prompt: Most people are now aware of the environmental damage caused by air travel, yet the number of flights taken each year continues to rise. Why do people keep flying? What should be done about this?
essay:
Air travel is one of the few forms of consumption whose environmental cost is widely understood and yet almost universally ignored. Passenger numbers have grown for decades despite constant publicity about emissions, and the explanation lies in economics and in psychology rather than in ignorance.

The economic half is straightforward. Aviation fuel is untaxed in most jurisdictions and international tickets usually escape sales tax, so a seat on a plane is priced well below the cost it imposes on everyone else. When a flight across a continent costs less than a rail ticket over the same route, consumers are not choosing to pollute; they are choosing the cheaper of two options, and the price signal is telling them the wrong thing.

The psychological half concerns scale. An individual passenger knows that their absence would not ground the aircraft, so the connection between the decision and the damage feels theoretical. Flying is also concentrated in exactly those parts of life people are least willing to sacrifice — seeing relatives abroad, a holiday earned over a year, work that cannot be done remotely — and abstract responsibility rarely wins against a specific and immediate reason to travel.

Effective policy therefore has to change the price rather than the attitude. Taxing aviation fuel on the same basis as petrol, and adding a levy that rises steeply with the number of flights a person takes in a year, would target frequent travellers without penalising the family that flies once. The revenue could then be used to make rail competitive on short routes, where the alternative already exists and only the cost prevents people from using it.

Individuals will not solve this by feeling guilty. They will change when the cheapest option stops being the most damaging one.
title: Why people keep flying despite the climate cost
